summary.text: 六 is the numeral ‘six,’ attested in oracle-bone records as a cardinal number and in a month name. Its graphic origin is disputed: proposals include a shelter picture, a conventional counting mark, or an early graph similar to 入.

formation.text: The graph’s formation is disputed. One account treats the whole form as a pictograph of a simple shelter; other proposals treat it as a conventional counting mark or as a graph once similar to 入 and later distinguished. The Shuowen analysis through 入 and 八 in 易 numerology is a historical interpretation that the paleographic discussion considers unlikely to preserve the original graphic meaning.

history.text: The oracle-script-style and Western Zhou bronze-script-style images are modern reconstructions labeled for different script traditions. They provide examples of those styles, but do not establish a sequence of graphic changes or settle the graph’s origin.
The Shuowen explanation connects 六 with 入 and 八 through 易 numerology; this is a historical account, not a demonstrated graphic breakdown.

uncertainties.text: The graphic origin remains unresolved among proposals that 六 was once similar to 入, depicted a shelter associated with 廬, or served as a conventional counting mark. The cited numeral uses do not decide among them.

The proposed borrowing from a shelter word is unconfirmed: the shelter’s name and pronunciation are not independently established, and the cited Old Chinese reconstructions for 六 and 廬 do not substantiate a sound match.

senses.text: Cited oracle-bone records use 六 as a cardinal numeral in “six sheep” and in a month name meaning “sixth month.” They attest both uses but do not establish which came first.

limitations.text: The earliest cited evidence already uses 六 as a numeral. A prior shelter meaning and a transition from that meaning to ‘six’ are not established; the proposed sound-based borrowing remains unconfirmed.
The relative chronology of the cardinal and ordinal uses is unresolved.

relationships.text: Cited oracle-bone records use 六 as a cardinal numeral in “six sheep” and in a month name meaning “sixth month.” They attest both uses but do not establish which came first.

overview.text: 六 is a single graph meaning “six,” with no supported present-day component split. Oracle-bone records already use it as a numeral, but its original graphic explanation remains disputed.

takeaway.text: A shelter picture reused for ‘six’ because its name sounded similar is only a proposal; the shelter’s name and sound match are unconfirmed.

evidence.text: Originally a pictograph of a tent or building. Unrelated to modern meaning.
《易》之數，陰變於六，正於八。从入从八。凡六之屬皆从六。

Pictogram (象形) – perhaps a shed. Originally using the similar-sounding word 廬 (OC *ra, “shed, cabin”) to represent the concept “six” (Liu Xinglong). Alternatively, it may be an ancient counting symbol.
From Proto-Sino-Tibetan *d-k-ruk (“six”).

evidence.source: 漢語多功能字庫 (CUHK Multi-function Chinese Character Database)
evidence.field: 漢字甲骨部件分析：六; lines 122–127
evidence.text: The database reports competing explanations: early 六 and 入 are graphically alike and may once have been one graph, with added strokes later distinguishing the numeral; another proposal treats 六 as a shelter picture and an earlier graph for 廬; a third treats it as a conventional early counting mark. It regards the Shuowen explanation through 易 numerology as unlikely to preserve the graph’s original meaning. It cites oracle-bone numeral uses as cardinal in 合集 32320 (‘燎六羊’) and ordinal in 合集 7775 (‘今六月王入于商’), then gives numeral examples from bronzes and Warring States texts. These citations support numeral use in the cited oracle-bone records, not a chronology among the proposed graphic origins.
evidence.title: 漢字甲骨部件分析：六

evidence.source: 字源考釋 - 六, 香港教育城相關字源資源
evidence.text: The page labels a sequence of oracle-bone, bronze, small-seal, and standard forms, and says the first three resemble a front view of a shelter, the original graph for 廬, later borrowed for the number six. The page supplies no argument dating this interpretation or evidence for the pronunciation of the supposed shelter name. Its images were not visually inspected here.
evidence.title: 字源考釋 - 六

evidence.source: William H. Baxter and Laurent Sagart
evidence.field: Old Chinese reconstruction table and system notes; lines 0–34, 108 and 217
evidence.text: In Baxter–Sagart Old Chinese version 1.1 (2014), 六 has Mandarin liù, Middle Chinese transcription ljuwk, and Old Chinese *k.ruk, gloss ‘six’; 廬 has Mandarin lú, Middle Chinese transcription ljo, and Old Chinese *[r]a, gloss ‘hut; inn; to lodge’. The authors describe MC as a transcription based on historical sources, not a reconstruction, and say brackets mark uncertainty. These character-word entries do not independently establish that the object depicted by 六 was called 廬; the compared reconstructions do not substantiate the proposed sound-based loan. The local row checked for 六 in sources/baxter-sagart/baxtersagart.tsv, row 2140, agrees with the published table.
evidence.kind: primary reconstruction table and system description
evidence.title: Baxter-Sagart Old Chinese reconstruction, version 1.1 (13 September 2014)

evidence.text: This secondary character entry calls the origin unclear and summarizes a possible 入 differentiation account and a hut pictograph thought to be the earlier form of 廬; it says the numeral meaning is a phonetic loan under either account. It labels oracle script (~1250–1000 BC), early Western Zhou bronze (~1000 BC), Shuowen seal (~100 AD), and Eastern Han clerical exemplars. These labels date displayed script examples, not the origin of the numeral sense. Its historical pronunciation table gives *k.ruk, ljuwk, liù.
evidence.title: 六 - Dong Chinese dictionary

evidence.source: Kotobank, 精選版 日本国語大辞典 and 普及版 字通
evidence.field: 六: dated examples; character form and readings; lines 56–73 and 104–123
evidence.text: The dictionary records Japanese むゆ in a Nihon Shoki example dated 720 (the cited manuscript reading tradition), and in 年中行事秘抄 from the late 12th century. It records ろく for ‘six’ in a late-8th-century Man'yōshū example. These date Japanese lexical attestations, not the Chinese graph’s origin. 字通 endorses a small-shelter interpretation of oracle-bone and bronze forms, says the graph was borrowed for six, and notes that the seal form is not the graph’s initial form; this remains one account among competing proposals.
evidence.kind: historical dictionary with dated Japanese attestations and paleographic account
evidence.title: 六（読み）ロク - コトバンク

evidence.text: The 六 entry identifies the graph as a pictograph resembling a simple shelter. It says Shang oracle-bone forms resemble a shelter set on the ground and later forms emphasize the shelter wall; Qin small-seal form curves the two upper strokes inward, and clerical transformation changes them into a dot and horizontal stroke. It proposes a grass hut as the original meaning and 六 as an early graph for 廬, later borrowed for the numeral because the sounds were close. It also connects 六 with the yin line in the Changes. editorial_rules: Write about the character's graphic history; distinguish it from the history of a spoken word.
Separate historical explanation from mnemonics. Do not infer history from modern shapes or readings.
Sources may repeat one another. A source count is not independent corroboration.
Treat Shuowen as a historical account, not automatic confirmation. Its generated English glosses are excluded.
Unrelated word senses may appear in Wiktionary excerpts. Do not merge them into a character origin.
Related-character evidence retains its record_character. Do not silently transfer a traditional form's components to a simplified form.
No glyph image has been visually inspected in this packet. Do not claim to have inspected one.
Explain missing evidence explicitly, especially for Japanese-created characters. A Chinese spelling pronunciation is not evidence for a Japanese origin.

search_audit.query: 六 甲骨文 入 屋舍 字源 六 廬 字源 字源考释
search_audit.outcome: Search surfaced the CUHK paleographic entry, the Hong Kong Education City 六 page, and comparative references. I opened the CUHK, Education City, and Baxter–Sagart sources; un-opened results are treated only as discovery leads.

search_audit.outcome: Opened the primary reconstruction PDF and inspected its system notes and table. The comparison lists 六 *k.ruk and 廬 *[r]a; the object depicted in the shelter proposal is not named independently by this table.

search_audit.query: 六 kMandarin Unicode Unihan U+516D; six 六 oracle bone inscription 32320 六羊 oracle period paleographic
search_audit.outcome: Search results exposed secondary Unicode lookups and the Academia Sinica character record. I opened the Academia Sinica page and attempted the official Unicode endpoint, which returned an internal error. I did not treat third-party kMandarin reporting as the required official per-character verification.

gaps: The graphic origin remains unresolved: sources report the 入-related differentiation proposal, a shelter/廬 proposal, and a conventional counting-mark possibility. The inscriptions cited by CUHK support numeral use but do not settle which graphic account is correct.

The shelter-name hypothesis is not phonologically established. The object/name is not independently recovered, and Baxter–Sagart lists distinct reconstructed forms for 六 and 廬. This does not disprove every possible proposal, but does not support a sound-based borrowing from 廬.

CUHK cites oracle-bone records 合集 32320 and 7775 for cardinal and ordinal uses, but the original inscription images and exact excavation/inscription dates were not inspected. The earliest semantic transition and chronology between cardinal and ordinal use remain unestablished.

Later graphic stages and any specific graphic corruption were not established by visual inspection. Online entries label stages or provide inaccessible-to-text glyph images; no specific transformation should be asserted from this run.

The required Unicode Unihan per-character records for 六 (U+516D) and 廬 (U+5EEC) could not be accessed. The local Unihan row liù is not emitted as externally verified evidence; the accessible official Taiwanese record supports modern Mandarin liù for 六 only.

No independent early dated Chinese lexical evidence beyond the cited oracle-bone examples was opened. Japanese dated uses are later language-specific evidence and do not date the Chinese graph’s origin.

The graph’s origin remains unresolved among the 入-differentiation, shelter/廬, and counting-mark proposals. The consulted primary paleographic entry reports these as alternatives; the numeral-use examples do not decide among them.

The proposed shelter-name borrowing is not independently established: the depicted object’s name and pronunciation are unrecovered in the inspected evidence. The proposed loan from 廬 therefore remains unsupported as a sound-based explanation; no pronunciation match is inferred here.

CUHK cites oracle-bone cardinal and ordinal examples, but the original inscription images and exact dates of the individual records were not inspected. Their relative semantic chronology remains open.

The opened official Unihan endpoint for 六 was inaccessible, and the required current kMandarin reading was not verified from that record. The Taiwan CNS11643 record supports liù as modern Mandarin metadata only.
No exact character-specific Xiaoxuetang result or inspectable CC0 notice was retrieved in this run. Commons pages support the proposed image candidates and their stated licensing instead.

The proposed Commons images are modern digital drawings of ancient script forms, not photos of inscribed artifacts. Their labels indicate script traditions; the candidate files do not independently settle the graphic origin.

The 六 entry in 李學勤主編《字源》 was directly inspected on the supplied continuation scan: PDF page 1282, printed page 1267. The previous supplied scan is PDF page 1281, printed page 1266; it contains the 六 department heading and pronunciation lead but not the substantive 六 explanation. The corpus metadata lacks extracted printed-page numbers, but the printed numbers 1266 and 1267 are legible in the scans.

The graphic origin remains unsettled among differentiation from 入, a shelter/廬 proposal, and a conventional counting-mark proposal. The oracle-bone numeral examples cited by CUHK attest numeral use, not which origin account is correct.

The proposed hut-name borrowing is not independently established. The identity and pronunciation of the alleged depicted object are unrecovered in inspected evidence; Baxter–Sagart’s listed reconstructions for 六 and 廬 do not substantiate the suggested sound match.

CUHK cites cardinal and ordinal oracle-bone records, but I did not inspect the original inscription images or establish the precise dates of those individual records. Their relative chronology remains unresolved.

The original page 1282 scan was directly inspected from the local book repository; the supplied attachment itself contains page 1281 only. The image inspection is therefore of the repository scan, not of a supplied page-1282 attachment.

The required official Unicode per-character record for 六 returned an internal error. Local current-reading metadata exists, and an Academia Sinica record was opened, but neither is the mandated official Unihan click-through evidence.

items.period: Shang oracle-script style; the file page points to Sinica record 43.F555, 合137 賓組
items.tradition: Oracle-bone script style; modern vector reconstruction
items.caption: An oracle-script-style reconstruction of 六, whose early numeral use is cited in oracle-bone records. Its original graphic explanation remains disputed.
items.alt: Black, tent-like glyph with a pointed top and two descending strokes, reconstructed in oracle-script style.
items.selection_reason: Its shelter-like outline makes the candidate relevant to one proposed graphic interpretation, while the inscriptional examples establish numeral use without settling the graph’s origin.
items.rights: CC0 1.0 / public domain as stated on the Commons file page; attribution appreciated.

items.tradition: Bronze script style; modern vector reconstruction
items.caption: A bronze-script-style reconstruction of 六, presented as a Western Zhou form. It provides a comparison with the oracle-script-style candidate, but does not establish a sequence of graphic changes.
items.alt: Black glyph with a central upright and branching curved strokes, reconstructed in bronze-script style.
items.selection_reason: The visibly different form provides a useful comparison of script styles; the evidence labels it Western Zhou but does not document its exact relationship to the other candidate.
items.rights: CC0 1.0 / public domain as stated on the Commons file page; attribution appreciated.

limitations.text: Both images are modern digital reconstructions, not photographs of inscribed artifacts. Their script-style labels do not establish the character’s origin or a specific path of graphic change.

The graph’s origin remains unresolved among proposals relating it to 入, depicting a shelter associated with 廬, or serving as a conventional counting mark. The cited numeral uses do not decide among these explanations.
